T1003.001.subject: C0014
T1003.001.text: During Operation Wocao, threat actors used ProcDump to dump credentials from memory.

T1003.001.subject: C0025
T1003.001.text: During the 2016 Ukraine Electric Power Attack, Sandworm Team used Mimikatz to capture and use legitimate credentials.

T1003.001.subject: C0029
T1003.001.text: During Cutting Edge, threat actors used Task Manager to dump LSASS memory from Windows devices to disk.

T1003.001.subject: C0030
T1003.001.text: In the Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack, TEMP.Veles used Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: C0032
T1003.001.text: During the C0032 campaign, TEMP.Veles used Mimikatz and a custom tool, SecHack, to harvest credentials.

T1003.001.subject: C0038
T1003.001.text: During HomeLand Justice, threat actors dumped LSASS memory on compromised hosts.

T1003.001.subject: C0058
T1003.001.text: During SharePoint ToolShell Exploitation, threat actors used Mimikatz to dump LSASS memory.

T1003.001.subject: C0061
T1003.001.text: During Operation Digital Eye, threat actors targeted memory from the LSASS process to extract credentials.

T1003.001.subject: C0063
T1003.001.text: During the 2025 Poland Wiper Attacks, the adversaries attempted to dump credentials utilizing LSASS.

T1003.001.subject: G0003
T1003.001.text: Cleaver has been known to dump credentials using Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor.

T1003.001.subject: G0004
T1003.001.text: Ke3chang has dumped credentials, including by using Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G0006
T1003.001.text: APT1 has been known to use credential dumping using Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G0007
T1003.001.text: APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims. They have also dumped the LSASS process memory using the MiniDump function.

T1003.001.subject: G0022
T1003.001.text: APT3 has used a tool to dump credentials by injecting itself into lsass.exe and triggering with the argument "dig."

T1003.001.subject: G0027
T1003.001.text: Threat Group-3390 actors have used a modified version of Mimikatz called Wrapikatz to dump credentials. They have also dumped credentials from domain controllers.

T1003.001.subject: G0034
T1003.001.text: Sandworm Team has used its plainpwd tool, a modified version of Mimikatz, and comsvcs.dll to dump Windows credentials from system memory.

T1003.001.subject: G0037
T1003.001.text: FIN6 has used Windows Credential Editor for credential dumping.

T1003.001.subject: G0049
T1003.001.text: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as Mimikatz to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.

T1003.001.subject: G0050
T1003.001.text: APT32 used Mimikatz and customized versions of Windows Credential Dumper to harvest credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G0059
T1003.001.text: Magic Hound has stolen domain credentials by dumping LSASS process memory using Task Manager, comsvcs.dll, and from a Microsoft Active Directory Domain Controller using Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G0060
T1003.001.text: BRONZE BUTLER has used various tools (such as Mimikatz and WCE) to perform credential dumping.

T1003.001.subject: G0061
T1003.001.text: FIN8 harvests credentials using Invoke-Mimikatz or Windows Credentials Editor (WCE).

T1003.001.subject: G0064
T1003.001.text: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne, Mimikatz, and ProcDump to dump credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G0065
T1003.001.text: Leviathan has used publicly available tools to dump password hashes, including ProcDump and WCE.

T1003.001.subject: G0068
T1003.001.text: PLATINUM has used keyloggers that are also capable of dumping credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G0069
T1003.001.text: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with Mimikatz and procdump64.exe.

T1003.001.subject: G0077
T1003.001.text: Leafminer used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne and Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G0087
T1003.001.text: APT39 has used Mimikatz, Windows Credential Editor and ProcDump to dump credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G0091
T1003.001.text: Silence has used the Farse6.1 utility (based on Mimikatz) to extract credentials from lsass.exe.

T1003.001.subject: G0093
T1003.001.text: GALLIUM used a modified version of Mimikatz along with a PowerShell-based Mimikatz to dump credentials on the victim machines.

T1003.001.subject: G0094
T1003.001.text: Kimsuky has gathered credentials using Mimikatz and ProcDump.

T1003.001.subject: G0096
T1003.001.text: APT41 has used hashdump, Mimikatz, Procdump, and the Windows Credential Editor to dump password hashes from memory and authenticate to other user accounts.

T1003.001.subject: G0102
T1003.001.text: Wizard Spider has dumped the lsass.exe memory to harvest credentials with the use of open-source tool LaZagne.

T1003.001.subject: G0107
T1003.001.text: Whitefly has used Mimikatz to obtain credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G0108
T1003.001.text: Blue Mockingbird has used Mimikatz to retrieve credentials from LSASS memory.

T1003.001.subject: G0117
T1003.001.text: Fox Kitten has used prodump to dump credentials from LSASS.

T1003.001.subject: G0119
T1003.001.text: Indrik Spider used Cobalt Strike to carry out credential dumping using ProcDump.

T1003.001.subject: G0125
T1003.001.text: HAFNIUM has used procdump to dump the LSASS process memory.

T1003.001.subject: G0129
T1003.001.text: Mustang Panda has harvested credentials from memory of lssas.exe with Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G0143
T1003.001.text: Aquatic Panda has attempted to harvest credentials through LSASS memory dumping.

T1003.001.subject: G1003
T1003.001.text: Ember Bear uses legitimate Sysinternals tools such as procdump to dump LSASS memory.

T1003.001.subject: G1006
T1003.001.text: Earth Lusca has used ProcDump to obtain the hashes of credentials by dumping the memory of the LSASS process.

T1003.001.subject: G1016
T1003.001.text: FIN13 has obtained memory dumps with ProcDump to parse and extract credentials from a victim's LSASS process memory with Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: G1017
T1003.001.text: Volt Typhoon has attempted to access hashed credentials from the LSASS process memory space.

T1003.001.subject: G1023
T1003.001.text: APT5 has used the Task Manager process to target LSASS process memory in order to obtain NTLM password hashes. APT5 has also dumped clear text passwords and hashes from memory using Mimikatz hosted through an RDP mapped drive.

T1003.001.subject: G1030
T1003.001.text: Agrius used tools such as Mimikatz to dump LSASS memory to capture credentials in victim environments.

T1003.001.subject: G1036
T1003.001.text: Moonstone Sleet retrieved credentials from LSASS memory.

T1003.001.subject: G1039
T1003.001.text: RedCurl used LaZagne to obtain passwords from memory.

T1003.001.subject: G1040
T1003.001.text: Play has used Mimikatz and the Windows Task Manager to dump LSASS process memory.

T1003.001.subject: G1048
T1003.001.text: UNC3886 has used MiniDump to dump process memory and search for cleartext credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G1051
T1003.001.text: Medusa Group has leveraged Mimikatz to dump LSASS to harvest credentials.

T1003.001.subject: G1054
T1003.001.text: MirrorFace has dumped LSASS memory for credential access.

T1003.001.subject: G1055
T1003.001.text: VOID MANTICORE has dumped LSASS credentials using `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32.exe`.

T1003.001.subject: S0002
T1003.001.text: Mimikatz performs credential dumping to obtain account and password information useful in gaining access to additional systems and enterprise network resources. It contains functionality to acquire information about credentials in many ways, including from the LSASS Memory.

T1003.001.subject: S0005
T1003.001.text: Windows Credential Editor can dump credentials.

T1003.001.subject: S0046
T1003.001.text: CozyCar has executed Mimikatz to harvest stored credentials from the victim and further victim penetration.

T1003.001.subject: S0056
T1003.001.text: Net Crawler uses credential dumpers such as Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor to extract cached credentials from Windows systems.

T1003.001.subject: S0121
T1003.001.text: Lslsass can dump active logon session password hashes from the lsass process.

T1003.001.subject: S0154
T1003.001.text: Cobalt Strike can spawn a job to inject into LSASS memory and dump password hashes.

T1003.001.subject: S0187
T1003.001.text: Daserf leverages Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor to steal credentials.

T1003.001.subject: S0192
T1003.001.text: Pupy can execute Lazagne as well as Mimikatz using PowerShell.

T1003.001.subject: S0194
T1003.001.text: PowerSploit contains a collection of Exfiltration modules that can harvest credentials using Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: S0342
T1003.001.text: GreyEnergy has a module for Mimikatz to collect Windows credentials from the victim’s machine.

T1003.001.subject: S0349
T1003.001.text: LaZagne can perform credential dumping from memory to obtain account and password information.

T1003.001.subject: S0357
T1003.001.text: SecretsDump and Mimikatz modules within Impacket can perform credential dumping to obtain account and password information.

T1003.001.subject: S0363
T1003.001.text: Empire contains an implementation of Mimikatz to gather credentials from memory.

T1003.001.subject: S0365
T1003.001.text: Olympic Destroyer contains a module that tries to obtain credentials from LSASS, similar to Mimikatz. These credentials are used with PsExec and Windows Management Instrumentation to help the malware propagate itself across a network.

T1003.001.subject: S0367
T1003.001.text: Emotet has been observed dropping and executing password grabber modules including Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: S0368
T1003.001.text: NotPetya contains a modified version of Mimikatz to help gather credentials that are later used for lateral movement.

T1003.001.subject: S0378
T1003.001.text: PoshC2 contains an implementation of Mimikatz to gather credentials from memory.

T1003.001.subject: S0428
T1003.001.text: PoetRAT used voStro.exe, a compiled pypykatz (Python version of Mimikatz), to steal credentials.

T1003.001.subject: S0439
T1003.001.text: Okrum was seen using MimikatzLite to perform credential dumping.

T1003.001.subject: S0583
T1003.001.text: Pysa can perform OS credential dumping using Mimikatz.

T1003.001.subject: S0606
T1003.001.text: Bad Rabbit has used Mimikatz to harvest credentials from the victim's machine.

T1003.001.subject: S0633
T1003.001.text: Sliver has a built-in `procdump` command allowing for retrieval of memory from processes such as `lsass.exe` for credential harvesting.

T1003.001.subject: S0681
T1003.001.text: Lizar can run Mimikatz to harvest credentials.

T1003.001.subject: S0692
T1003.001.text: SILENTTRINITY can create a memory dump of LSASS via the `MiniDumpWriteDump Win32` API call.

T1003.001.subject: S1060
T1003.001.text: Mafalda can dump password hashes from `LSASS.exe`.

T1003.001.subject: S1242
T1003.001.text: Qilin can employ an embedded Mimikatz module to dump LSASS memory.

T1003.005.subject: G0049
T1003.005.text: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.

T1003.005.subject: G0064
T1003.005.text: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.

T1003.005.subject: G0069
T1003.005.text: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.

T1003.005.subject: G0077
T1003.005.text: Leafminer used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne.

T1003.005.subject: S0119
T1003.005.text: Cachedump can extract cached password hashes from cache entry information.

T1003.005.subject: S0192
T1003.005.text: Pupy can use Lazagne for harvesting credentials.

T1003.005.subject: S0349
T1003.005.text: LaZagne can perform credential dumping from MSCache to obtain account and password information.

T1003.005.subject: S0439
T1003.005.text: Okrum was seen using modified Quarks PwDump to perform credential dumping.

T1021.002.text: The Regin malware platform can use Windows admin shares to move laterally.

T1021.002.subject: S0029
T1021.002.text: PsExec, a tool that has been used by adversaries, writes programs to the ADMIN$ network share to execute commands on remote systems.

T1021.002.subject: S0038
T1021.002.text: Adversaries can instruct Duqu to spread laterally by copying itself to shares it has enumerated and for which it has obtained legitimate credentials (via keylogging or other means). The remote host is then infected by using the compromised credentials to schedule a task on remote machines that executes the malware.

T1021.002.subject: S0039
T1021.002.text: Lateral movement can be done with Net through net use commands to connect to the on remote systems.

T1021.002.subject: S0056
T1021.002.text: Net Crawler uses Windows admin shares to establish authenticated sessions to remote systems over SMB as part of lateral movement.

T1021.002.subject: S0089
T1021.002.text: BlackEnergy has run a plug-in on a victim to spread through the local network by using PsExec and accessing admin shares.

T1021.002.subject: S0140
T1021.002.text: Shamoon accesses network share(s), enables share access to the target device, copies an executable payload to the target system, and uses a Scheduled Task/Job to execute the malware.

T1021.002.subject: S0154
T1021.002.text: Cobalt Strike can use Window admin shares (C$ and ADMIN$) for lateral movement.

T1021.002.subject: S0236
T1021.002.text: Kwampirs copies itself over network shares to move laterally on a victim network.

T1021.002.subject: S0350
T1021.002.text: zwShell has been copied over network shares to move laterally.

T1021.002.subject: S0365
T1021.002.text: Olympic Destroyer uses PsExec to interact with the ADMIN$ network share to execute commands on remote systems.

T1021.002.subject: S0367
T1021.002.text: Emotet has leveraged the Admin$, C$, and IPC$ shares for lateral movement.

T1021.002.subject: S0368
T1021.002.text: NotPetya can use PsExec, which interacts with the ADMIN$ network share to execute commands on remote systems.

T1021.002.subject: S0446
T1021.002.text: Ryuk has used the C$ network share for lateral movement.

T1021.002.subject: S0504
T1021.002.text: Anchor can support windows execution via SMB shares.

T1021.002.subject: S0532
T1021.002.text: Lucifer can infect victims by brute forcing SMB.

T1021.002.subject: S0575
T1021.002.text: Conti can spread via SMB and encrypts files on different hosts, potentially compromising an entire network.

T1021.002.subject: S0603
T1021.002.text: Stuxnet propagates to available network shares.

T1021.002.subject: S0608
T1021.002.text: Conficker variants spread through NetBIOS share propagation.

T1021.002.subject: S0659
T1021.002.text: Diavol can spread throughout a network via SMB prior to encryption.

T1021.002.subject: S0672
T1021.002.text: Zox has the ability to use SMB for communication.

T1021.002.subject: S0698
T1021.002.text: HermeticWizard can use a list of hardcoded credentials to to authenticate via NTLMSSP to the SMB shares on remote systems.

T1021.002.subject: S1063
T1021.002.text: Brute Ratel C4 has the ability to use SMB to pivot in compromised networks.

T1021.002.subject: S1073
T1021.002.text: Royal can use SMB to connect to move laterally.

T1021.002.subject: S1180
T1021.002.text: BlackByte Ransomware uses mapped shared folders to transfer ransomware payloads via SMB.

T1021.002.subject: S1187
T1021.002.text: reGeorg has the ability to tunnel SMB sessions.

T1021.002.subject: S1199
T1021.002.text: LockBit 2.0 has the ability to move laterally via SMB.

T1021.002.subject: S1202
T1021.002.text: LockBit 3.0 can use SMB for lateral movement.

T1021.002.subject: S1212
T1021.002.text: RansomHub can use credentials provided in its configuration to move laterally from the infected machine over SMBv2.

T1021.002.subject: S1242
T1021.002.text: Qilin can embed a copy of PsExec within its payload and place it in the %Temp% directory under a randomly generated filename.

T1021.006.subject: C0024
T1021.006.text: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used WinRM via PowerShell to execute commands and payloads on remote hosts.

T1021.006.subject: C0048
T1021.006.text: During Operation MidnightEclipse, threat actors used WinRM to move laterally in targeted networks.

T1021.006.subject: G0027
T1021.006.text: Threat Group-3390 has used WinRM to enable remote execution.

T1021.006.subject: G0102
T1021.006.text: Wizard Spider has used Window Remote Management to move laterally through a victim network.

T1021.006.subject: G0114
T1021.006.text: Chimera has used WinRM for lateral movement.

T1021.006.subject: G1016
T1021.006.text: FIN13 has leveraged `WMI` to move laterally within a compromised network via application servers and SQL servers.

T1021.006.subject: G1053
T1021.006.text: Storm-0501 has utilized the post-exploitation tool known as Evil-WinRM that uses PowerShell over Windows Remote Management (WinRM) for remote code execution.

T1021.006.subject: S0154
T1021.006.text: Cobalt Strike can use WinRM to execute a payload on a remote host.

T1021.006.subject: S0692
T1021.006.text: SILENTTRINITY tracks `TrustedHosts` and can move laterally to these targets via WinRM.

T1021.006.subject: S1063
T1021.006.text: Brute Ratel C4 can use WinRM for pivoting.

T1027.subject: C0015
T1027.text: During C0015, the threat actors used Base64-encoded strings.

T1027.subject: C0017
T1027.text: During C0017, APT41 broke malicious binaries, including DEADEYE and KEYPLUG, into multiple sections on disk to evade detection.

T1027.subject: C0025
T1027.text: During the 2016 Ukraine Electric Power Attack, Sandworm Team used heavily obfuscated code with Industroyer in its Windows Notepad backdoor.

T1027.subject: C0057
T1027.text: During the 3CX Supply Chain Attack, AppleJeus payloads use AES-256 GCM cipher to encrypt data to include ICONICSTEALER and VEILEDSIGNAL.

T1027.subject: G0004
T1027.text: Ke3chang has used Base64-encoded shellcode strings.

T1027.subject: G0022
T1027.text: APT3 obfuscates files or information to help evade defensive measures.

T1027.subject: G0034
T1027.text: Sandworm Team has used Base64 encoding within malware variants.

T1027.subject: G0047
T1027.text: Gamaredon Group has delivered self-extracting 7z archive files within malicious document attachments. Additionally, Gamaredon Group has used an obfuscated .drv file.

T1027.subject: G0063
T1027.text: BlackOasis's first stage shellcode contains a NOP sled with alternative instructions that was likely designed to bypass antivirus tools.

T1027.subject: G0067
T1027.text: APT37 obfuscates strings and payloads.

T1027.subject: G0084
T1027.text: Gallmaker obfuscated shellcode used during execution.

T1027.subject: G0093
T1027.text: GALLIUM used a modified version of HTRAN in which they obfuscated strings such as debug messages in an apparent attempt to evade detection.

T1027.subject: G0094
T1027.text: Kimsuky has obfuscated binary strings including the use of XOR encryption and Base64 encoding. Kimsuky has also modified the first byte of DLL implants targeting victims to prevent recognition of the executable file format. Kimsuky has obfuscated strings using Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) instructions that complicate static analysis.

T1027.subject: G0096
T1027.text: APT41 used VMProtected binaries in multiple intrusions.

T1027.subject: G0099
T1027.text: APT-C-36 has used ConfuserEx to obfuscate its variant of Imminent Monitor, compressed payloads and RAT packages, and password protected encrypted email attachments to avoid detection. APT-C-36 has also compressed initial droppers into ZIP, LHA and UUE formats.

T1027.subject: G0106
T1027.text: Rocke has modified UPX headers after packing files to break unpackers.

T1027.subject: G0112
T1027.text: Windshift has used string encoding with floating point calculations.

T1027.subject: G0129
T1027.text: Mustang Panda has delivered initial payloads hidden using archives and encoding measures. Mustang Panda has also utilized opaque predicates in payloads to hinder analysis.

T1027.subject: G0135
T1027.text: BackdoorDiplomacy has obfuscated tools and malware it uses with VMProtect.

T1027.subject: G1006
T1027.text: Earth Lusca used Base64 to encode strings.

T1027.subject: G1036
T1027.text: Moonstone Sleet delivers encrypted payloads in pieces that are then combined together to form a new portable executable (PE) file during installation.

T1027.subject: G1039
T1027.text: RedCurl has used malware with string encryption. RedCurl has also encrypted data and has encoded PowerShell commands using Base64. RedCurl has used `PyArmor` to obfuscate code execution of LaZagne. Additionally, RedCurl has obfuscated downloaded files by renaming them as commonly used tools and has used `echo`, instead of file names themselves, to execute files.

T1027.subject: S0012
T1027.text: PoisonIvy hides any strings related to its own indicators of compromise.

T1027.subject: S0013
T1027.text: PlugX can use API hashing and modify the names of strings to evade detection.

T1027.subject: S0030
T1027.text: Carbanak encrypts strings to make analysis more difficult.

T1027.subject: S0045
T1027.text: Most of the strings in ADVSTORESHELL are encrypted with an XOR-based algorithm; some strings are also encrypted with 3DES and reversed. API function names are also reversed, presumably to avoid detection in memory.

T1027.subject: S0051
T1027.text: MiniDuke can use control flow flattening to obscure code.

T1027.subject: S0062
T1027.text: The DustySky dropper uses a function to obfuscate the name of functions and other parts of the malware.

T1027.subject: S0063
T1027.text: SHOTPUT is obscured using XOR encoding and appended to a valid GIF file.

T1027.subject: S0070
T1027.text: HTTPBrowser's code may be obfuscated through structured exception handling and return-oriented programming.

T1027.subject: S0091
T1027.text: Epic heavily obfuscates its code to make analysis more difficult.

T1027.subject: S0094
T1027.text: Trojan.Karagany can base64 encode and AES-128-CBC encrypt data prior to transmission.

T1027.subject: S0117
T1027.text: A version of XTunnel introduced in July 2015 obfuscated the binary using opaque predicates and other techniques in a likely attempt to obfuscate it and bypass security products.

T1027.subject: S0124
T1027.text: Pisloader obfuscates files by splitting strings into smaller sub-strings and including "garbage" strings that are never used. The malware also uses return-oriented programming (ROP) technique and single-byte XOR to obfuscate data.

T1027.subject: S0126
T1027.text: ComRAT has encrypted its virtual file system using AES-256 in XTS mode.

T1027.subject: S0132
T1027.text: H1N1 uses multiple techniques to obfuscate strings, including XOR.

T1027.subject: S0137
T1027.text: CORESHELL obfuscates strings using a custom stream cipher.

T1027.subject: S0138
T1027.text: OLDBAIT obfuscates internal strings and unpacks them at startup.

T1027.subject: S0140
T1027.text: Shamoon contains base64-encoded strings.

T1027.subject: S0142
T1027.text: StreamEx obfuscates some commands by using statically programmed fragments of strings when starting a DLL. It also uses a one-byte xor against 0x91 to encode configuration data.

T1027.subject: S0148
T1027.text: RTM strings, network data, configuration, and modules are encrypted with a modified RC4 algorithm.

T1027.subject: S0150
T1027.text: POSHSPY appends a file signature header (randomly selected from six file types) to encrypted data prior to upload or download.

T1027.subject: S0154
T1027.text: Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata.

T1027.subject: S0167
T1027.text: Matryoshka obfuscates API function names using a substitute cipher combined with Base64 encoding.

T1027.subject: S0182
T1027.text: FinFisher is heavily obfuscated in many ways, including through the use of spaghetti code in its functions in an effort to confuse disassembly programs. It also uses a custom XOR algorithm to obfuscate code.

T1027.subject: S0187
T1027.text: Daserf uses encrypted Windows APIs and also encrypts data using the alternative base64+RC4 or the Caesar cipher.

T1027.subject: S0189
T1027.text: ISMInjector is obfuscated with the off-the-shelf SmartAssembly .NET obfuscator created by red-gate.com.

T1027.subject: S0196
T1027.text: PUNCHBUGGY has hashed most its code's functions and encrypted payloads with base64 and XOR.

T1027.subject: S0197
T1027.text: PUNCHTRACK is loaded and executed by a highly obfuscated launcher.

T1027.subject: S0198
T1027.text: NETWIRE has used a custom obfuscation algorithm to hide strings including Registry keys, APIs, and DLL names.

T1027.subject: S0201
T1027.text: A JPIN uses a encrypted and compressed payload that is disguised as a bitmap within the resource section of the installer.

T1027.subject: S0203
T1027.text: Hydraq uses basic obfuscation in the form of spaghetti code.

T1027.subject: S0229
T1027.text: Some Orz strings are base64 encoded, such as the embedded DLL known as MockDll.

T1027.subject: S0240
T1027.text: ROKRAT can encrypt data prior to exfiltration by using an RSA public key.

T1027.subject: S0242
T1027.text: SynAck payloads are obfuscated prior to compilation to inhibit analysis and/or reverse engineering.

T1027.subject: S0244
T1027.text: Comnie uses RC4 and Base64 to obfuscate strings.

T1027.subject: S0259
T1027.text: InnaputRAT uses an 8-byte XOR key to obfuscate API names and other strings contained in the payload.

T1027.subject: S0260
T1027.text: InvisiMole avoids analysis by encrypting all strings, internal files, configuration data and by using a custom executable format.

T1027.subject: S0264
T1027.text: OopsIE uses the Confuser protector to obfuscate an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2. OopsIE also encodes collected data in hexadecimal format before writing to files on disk and obfuscates strings.

T1027.subject: S0265
T1027.text: Kazuar is obfuscated using the open source ConfuserEx protector. Kazuar also obfuscates the name of created files/folders/mutexes and encrypts debug messages written to log files using the Rijndael cipher.

T1027.subject: S0266
T1027.text: TrickBot uses non-descriptive names to hide functionality.

T1027.subject: S0283
T1027.text: jRAT’s Java payload is encrypted with AES. Additionally, backdoor files are encrypted using DES as a stream cipher. Later variants of jRAT also incorporated AV evasion methods such as Java bytecode obfuscation via the commercial Allatori obfuscation tool.

T1027.subject: S0331
T1027.text: Agent Tesla has had its code obfuscated in an apparent attempt to make analysis difficult. Agent Tesla has used the Rijndael symmetric encryption algorithm to encrypt strings.

T1027.subject: S0332
T1027.text: Remcos uses RC4 and base64 to obfuscate data, including Registry entries and file paths. Remcos can also employ control flow flattening to hinder analysis.

T1027.subject: S0335
T1027.text: Carbon encrypts configuration files and tasks for the malware to complete using CAST-128 algorithm.

T1027.subject: S0336
T1027.text: NanoCore’s plugins were obfuscated with Eazfuscater.NET 3.3.

T1027.subject: S0353
T1027.text: NOKKI uses Base64 encoding for strings.

T1027.subject: S0354
T1027.text: Denis obfuscates its code and encrypts the API names.

T1027.subject: S0355
T1027.text: Final1stspy obfuscates strings with base64 encoding.

T1027.subject: S0369
T1027.text: CoinTicker initially downloads a hidden encoded file.

T1027.subject: S0377
T1027.text: Ebury has obfuscated its strings with a simple XOR encryption with a static key.

T1027.subject: S0384
T1027.text: Dridex's strings are obfuscated using RC4.

T1027.subject: S0393
T1027.text: PowerStallion uses a XOR cipher to encrypt command output written to its OneDrive C2 server.

T1027.subject: S0428
T1027.text: PoetRAT has used a custom encryption scheme for communication between scripts.

T1027.subject: S0434
T1027.text: Imminent Monitor has encrypted the spearphish attachments to avoid detection from email gateways; the debugger also encrypts information before sending to the C2.

T1027.subject: S0445
T1027.text: ShimRatReporter encrypted gathered information with a combination of shifting and XOR using a static key.

T1027.subject: S0446
T1027.text: Ryuk can use anti-disassembly and code transformation obfuscation techniques.

T1027.subject: S0447
T1027.text: Lokibot has obfuscated strings with base64 encoding.

T1027.subject: S0449
T1027.text: Maze has decrypted strings and other important information during the encryption process. Maze also calls certain functions dynamically to hinder analysis.

T1027.subject: S0458
T1027.text: Ramsay has base64-encoded its portable executable and hidden itself under a JPG header. Ramsay can also embed information within document footers.

T1027.subject: S0461
T1027.text: SDBbot has the ability to XOR the strings for its installer component with a hardcoded 128 byte key.

T1027.subject: S0465
T1027.text: CARROTBALL has used a custom base64 alphabet to decode files.

T1027.subject: S0467
T1027.text: TajMahal has used an encrypted Virtual File System to store plugins.

T1027.subject: S0476
T1027.text: Valak has the ability to base64 encode and XOR encrypt strings.

T1027.subject: S0482
T1027.text: Bundlore has obfuscated data with base64, AES, RC4, and bz2.

T1027.subject: S0499
T1027.text: Hancitor has used Base64 to encode malicious links.

T1027.subject: S0500
T1027.text: MCMD can Base64 encode output strings prior to sending to C2.

T1027.subject: S0502
T1027.text: Drovorub has used XOR encrypted payloads in WebSocket client to server messages.

T1027.subject: S0504
T1027.text: Anchor has obfuscated code with stack strings and string encryption.

T1027.subject: S0511
T1027.text: RegDuke can use control-flow flattening or the commercially available .NET Reactor for obfuscation.

T1027.subject: S0512
T1027.text: FatDuke can use base64 encoding, string stacking, and opaque predicates for obfuscation.

T1027.subject: S0516
T1027.text: SoreFang has the ability to encode and RC6 encrypt data sent to C2.

T1027.subject: S0517
T1027.text: Pillowmint has obfuscated the AES key used for encryption.

T1027.subject: S0518
T1027.text: PolyglotDuke can custom encrypt strings.

T1027.subject: S0559
T1027.text: SUNBURST obfuscated collected system information using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm.

T1027.subject: S0560
T1027.text: TEARDROP created and read from a file with a fake JPG header, and its payload was encrypted with a simple rotating XOR cipher.

T1027.subject: S0562
T1027.text: SUNSPOT encrypted log entries it collected with the stream cipher RC4 using a hard-coded key. It also uses AES128-CBC encrypted blobs for SUNBURST source code and data extracted from the SolarWinds Orion process.

T1027.subject: S0575
T1027.text: Conti can use compiler-based obfuscation for its code, encrypt DLLs, and hide Windows API calls.

T1027.subject: S0584
T1027.text: AppleJeus has XOR-encrypted collected system information prior to sending to a C2. AppleJeus has also used the open source ADVObfuscation library for its components.

T1027.subject: S0593
T1027.text: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON has encrypted strings with RC4.

T1027.subject: S0594
T1027.text: Out1 has the ability to encode data.

T1027.subject: S0596
T1027.text: ShadowPad has encrypted its payload, a virtual file system, and various files.

T1027.subject: S0598
T1027.text: P.A.S. Webshell can use encryption and base64 encoding to hide strings and to enforce access control once deployed.

T1027.subject: S0604
T1027.text: Industroyer uses heavily obfuscated code in its Windows Notepad backdoor.

T1027.subject: S0605
T1027.text: EKANS uses encoded strings in its process kill list.

T1027.subject: S0607
T1027.text: KillDisk uses VMProtect to make reverse engineering the malware more difficult.

T1027.subject: S0608
T1027.text: Conficker has obfuscated its code to prevent its removal from host machines.

T1027.subject: S0615
T1027.text: SombRAT can encrypt strings with XOR-based routines and use a custom AES storage format for plugins, configuration, C2 domains, and harvested data.

T1027.subject: S0622
T1027.text: AppleSeed has the ability to Base64 encode its payload and custom encrypt API calls.

T1027.subject: S0623
T1027.text: Siloscape itself is obfuscated and uses obfuscated API calls.

T1027.subject: S0624
T1027.text: Ecipekac can use XOR, AES, and DES to encrypt loader shellcode.

T1027.subject: S0625
T1027.text: Cuba has used multiple layers of obfuscation to avoid analysis, including its Base64 encoded payload.

T1027.subject: S0627
T1027.text: SodaMaster can use "stackstrings" for obfuscation.

T1027.subject: S0632
T1027.text: GrimAgent has used Rotate on Right (RoR) and Rotate on Left (RoL) functionality to encrypt strings.

T1027.subject: S0633
T1027.text: Sliver obfuscates configuration and other static files using native Go libraries such as `garble` and `gobfuscate` to inhibit configuration analysis and static detection.

T1027.subject: S0635
T1027.text: BoomBox can encrypt data using AES prior to exfiltration.

T1027.subject: S0640
T1027.text: Avaddon has used encrypted strings.

T1027.subject: S0641
T1027.text: Kobalos encrypts all strings using RC4 and bundles all functionality into a single function call.

T1027.subject: S0647
T1027.text: Turian can use VMProtect for obfuscation.

T1027.subject: S0650
T1027.text: QakBot has hidden code within Excel spreadsheets by turning the font color to white and splitting it across multiple cells.

T1027.subject: S0651
T1027.text: BoxCaon used the "StackStrings" obfuscation technique to hide malicious functionalities.

T1027.subject: S0659
T1027.text: Diavol has Base64 encoded the RSA public key used for encrypting files.

T1027.subject: S0660
T1027.text: The Clambling executable has been obfuscated when dropped on a compromised host.

T1027.subject: S0681
T1027.text: Lizar has obfuscated the fingerprint of the victim system, the local IP address, and the Fowler-Noll-V 1 (FNV-1) hash of the local IP address using an XOR operation. The data is then sent to the C2 server.

T1027.subject: S0690
T1027.text: Green Lambert has encrypted strings.

T1027.subject: S0694
T1027.text: DRATzarus can be partly encrypted with XOR.

T1027.subject: S0696
T1027.text: Flagpro has been delivered within ZIP or RAR password-protected archived files.

T1027.subject: S1018
T1027.text: Saint Bot has been obfuscated to help avoid detection.

T1027.subject: S1025
T1027.text: Amadey has obfuscated strings such as antivirus vendor names, domains, files, and others.

T1027.subject: S1028
T1027.text: Action RAT's commands, strings, and domains can be Base64 encoded within the payload.

T1027.subject: S1035
T1027.text: Small Sieve has the ability to use a custom hex byte swapping encoding scheme combined with an obfuscated Base64 function to protect program strings and Telegram credentials.

T1027.subject: S1039
T1027.text: Bumblebee has been delivered as password-protected zipped ISO files and used control-flow-flattening to obfuscate the flow of functions.

T1027.subject: S1053
T1027.text: AvosLocker has used XOR-encoded strings.

T1027.subject: S1063
T1027.text: Brute Ratel C4 has used encrypted payload files and maintains an encrypted configuration structure in memory.

T1027.subject: S1064
T1027.text: SVCReady can encrypt victim data with an RC4 cipher.

T1027.subject: S1066
T1027.text: DarkTortilla has been obfuscated with the DeepSea .NET and ConfuserEx code obfuscators.

T1027.subject: S1085
T1027.text: Sardonic can use certain ConfuserEx features for obfuscation and can be encoded in a base64 string.

T1027.subject: S1086
T1027.text: Snip3 has the ability to obfuscate strings using XOR encryption.

T1027.subject: S1090
T1027.text: NightClub can obfuscate strings using the congruential generator `(LCG): staten+1 = (690069 × staten + 1) mod 232`.

T1027.subject: S1099
T1027.text: Samurai can encrypt the names of requested APIs.

T1027.subject: S1104
T1027.text: SLOWPULSE can hide malicious code in the padding regions between legitimate functions in the Pulse Secure `libdsplibs.so` file.

T1027.subject: S1105
T1027.text: COATHANGER can store obfuscated configuration information in the last 56 bytes of the file `/date/.bd.key/preload.so`.

T1027.subject: S1111
T1027.text: DarkGate uses a hard-coded string as a seed, along with the victim machine hardware identifier and input text, to generate a unique string used as an internal mutex value to evade static detection based on mutexes.

T1027.subject: S1118
T1027.text: BUSHWALK can encrypt the resulting data generated from C2 commands with RC4.

T1027.subject: S1130
T1027.text: Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection.

T1027.subject: S1138
T1027.text: The Gootloader first stage script is obfuscated using random alpha numeric strings.

T1027.subject: S1149
T1027.text: CHIMNEYSWEEP can use a custom Base64 alphabet to encode an API decryption key.

T1027.subject: S1161
T1027.text: BPFDoor can require a password to activate the backdoor and uses RC4 encryption or static library encryption `libtomcrypt`.

T1027.subject: S1183
T1027.text: StrelaStealer has been distributed in ISO archives. StrelaStealer has been delivered in encrypted, password-protected ZIP archives.

T1027.subject: S1213
T1027.text: Lumma Stealer has used SmartAssembly to obfuscate .NET payloads.

T1027.subject: S1226
T1027.text: BOOKWORM has been delivered using self-extracting RAR archives.

T1027.subject: S1228
T1027.text: PUBLOAD has obfuscated DLL names using the ror13AddHash32 algorithm.

T1027.subject: S9007
T1027.text: HTTPTroy has obfuscated strings using Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) instructions to hinder analysis and detection.

T1027.subject: S9008

T1047.subject: C0001

T1047.subject: C0018
T1047.text: During C0018, the threat actors used WMIC to modify administrative settings on both a local and a remote host, likely as part of the first stages for their lateral movement; they also used WMI Provider Host (`wmiprvse.exe`) to execute a variety of encoded PowerShell scripts using the `DownloadString` method.

T1485.subject: C0034
T1485.text: During the 2022 Ukraine Electric Power Attack, Sandworm Team deployed CaddyWiper on the victim’s IT environment systems to wipe files related to the OT capabilities, along with mapped drives, and physical drive partitions.

T1485.subject: C0063
T1485.text: During the 2025 Poland Wiper Attacks, the adversaries utilized wiper malware to overwrite files using a 16-byte buffer that fully overwrites files 16 bytes or smaller or partially overwrites files greater than 16 bytes to speed up the process.

T1485.subject: G0032
T1485.text: Lazarus Group has used a custom secure delete function to overwrite file contents with data from heap memory.

T1485.subject: G0034
T1485.text: Sandworm Team has used CaddyWiper, SDelete, and the BlackEnergy KillDisk component to overwrite files on victim systems. Additionally, Sandworm Team has used the JUNKMAIL tool to overwrite files with null bytes.

T1485.subject: G0082
T1485.text: APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable.

T1485.subject: G1004
T1485.text: LAPSUS$ has deleted the target's systems and resources both on-premises and in the cloud.

T1485.subject: G1053
T1485.text: Storm-0501 has destroyed data and backup files.

T1485.subject: G1055
T1485.text: VOID MANTICORE has conducted data wiping attacks on compromised systems. VOID MANTICORE has also manually deleted files from compromised hosts, to include selecting all files and then deleting them.

T1485.subject: G1056
T1485.text: TeamPCP has deployed privileged DaemonSets to delete files on Kubernetes clusters and has executed recursive file deletions on non-containerized hosts.

T1485.subject: G1057
T1485.text: ShinyHunters has executed the `DeleteBucket` API call to delete buckets.

T1485.subject: S0089
T1485.text: BlackEnergy 2 contains a "Destroy" plug-in that destroys data stored on victim hard drives by overwriting file contents.

T1485.subject: S0139
T1485.text: PowerDuke has a command to write random data across a file and delete it.

T1485.subject: S0140
T1485.text: Shamoon attempts to overwrite operating system files and disk structures with image files. In a later variant, randomly generated data was used for data overwrites.

T1485.subject: S0195
T1485.text: SDelete deletes data in a way that makes it unrecoverable.

T1485.subject: S0238
T1485.text: Proxysvc can overwrite files indicated by the attacker before deleting them.

T1485.subject: S0265
T1485.text: Kazuar can overwrite files with random data before deleting them.

T1485.subject: S0341
T1485.text: Xbash has destroyed Linux-based databases as part of its ransomware capabilities.

T1485.subject: S0364
T1485.text: RawDisk was used in Shamoon to write to protected system locations such as the MBR and disk partitions in an effort to destroy data.

T1485.subject: S0365
T1485.text: Olympic Destroyer overwrites files locally and on remote shares.

T1485.subject: S0380
T1485.text: StoneDrill has a disk wiper module that targets files other than those in the Windows directory.

T1485.subject: S0496
T1485.text: REvil has the capability to destroy files and folders.

T1485.subject: S0604
T1485.text: Industroyer’s data wiper module clears registry keys and overwrites both ICS configuration and Windows files.

T1485.subject: S0607
T1485.text: KillDisk deletes system files to make the OS unbootable. KillDisk also targets and deletes files with 35 different file extensions.

T1485.subject: S0659
T1485.text: Diavol can delete specified files from a targeted system.

T1485.subject: S0688
T1485.text: Meteor can fill a victim's files and directories with zero-bytes in replacement of real content before deleting them.

T1485.subject: S0689
T1485.text: WhisperGate can corrupt files by overwriting the first 1 MB with `0xcc` and appending random extensions.

T1485.subject: S0693
T1485.text: CaddyWiper can work alphabetically through drives on a compromised system to take ownership of and overwrite all files.

T1485.subject: S0697
T1485.text: HermeticWiper can recursively wipe folders and files in `Windows`, `Program Files`, `Program Files(x86)`, `PerfLogs`, `Boot, System`, `Volume Information`, and `AppData` folders using `FSCTL_MOVE_FILE`. HermeticWiper can also overwrite symbolic links and big files in `My Documents` and on the Desktop with random bytes.

T1485.subject: S1125
T1485.text: AcidRain performs an in-depth wipe of the target filesystem and various attached storage devices through either a data overwrite or calling various IOCTLS to erase it.

T1485.subject: S1133
T1485.text: Apostle initially masqueraded as ransomware but actual functionality is a data destruction tool, supported by an internal name linked to an early version, wiper-action. Apostle writes random data to original files after an encrypted copy is created, along with resizing the original file to zero and changing time property metadata before finally deleting the original file.

T1485.subject: S1134
T1485.text: DEADWOOD overwrites files on victim systems with random data to effectively destroy them.

T1485.subject: S1135
T1485.text: MultiLayer Wiper deletes files on network drives, but corrupts and overwrites with random data files stored locally.

T1485.subject: S1167
T1485.text: AcidPour can perform an in-depth wipe of victim filesystems and attached storage devices through either data overwrite or calling various IOCTLS to erase them, similar to AcidRain.

T1485.subject: S1178
T1485.text: ShrinkLocker can initiate a destructive payload depending on the operating system check through resizing and reformatting portions of the victim machine's disk, leading to system instability and potential data corruption.

T1485.subject: S9008
T1485.text: Shai-Hulud has destroyed the victim’s home directory by overwriting and deleting every writable file within the user's home folder. Shai-Hulud has also utilized the `shred` command on Linux devices.

T1485.subject: S9030
T1485.text: SameCoin can overwrite designated files on targeted systems with random bytes.

T1485.subject: S9038
T1485.text: DynoWiper has overwritten files with 16-byte sequences of random data generated by the Mersenne Twister algorithm using the Microsoft Windows native `CreateFileW()` function to open the file and the `SetFilePointerEx()` and `WriteFile()` functions to overwrite the file. Additionally, versions of DynoWiper can also delete files using the `DeleteFileW` API.

T1485.subject: S9039
T1485.text: LazyWiper has overwritten files with pseudorandom 32‑byte sequences written at 16‑byte intervals making the file unrecoverable.

T1485.subject: S9042
T1485.text: CanisterWorm has targeted wiper components that can delete entire clusters and execute recursive file deletions on non-containerized hosts.

T1485.subject: S9043
T1485.text: Mini Shai-Hulud has wiped data on devices that fall within specified parameters to include those that resolve to specific geolocations including Iran and Israel. Mini Shai-Hulud has also implemented a dead-man’s switch that wipes the victims home directory if the operator revokes a GitHub token created by the adversary.

T1486.subject: C0015
T1486.text: During C0015, the threat actors used Conti ransomware to encrypt a compromised network.

T1486.subject: C0018
T1486.text: During C0018, the threat actors used AvosLocker ransomware to encrypt files on the compromised network.

T1486.subject: C0038
T1486.text: During HomeLand Justice, threat actors used ROADSWEEP ransomware to encrypt files on targeted systems.

T1486.subject: C0058
T1486.text: During SharePoint ToolShell Exploitation, threat actors deployed ransomware including 4L4MD4R and Warlock.

T1486.subject: G0034
T1486.text: Sandworm Team has used Prestige ransomware to encrypt data at targeted organizations in transportation and related logistics industries in Ukraine and Poland.

T1486.subject: G0046
T1486.text: FIN7 has encrypted virtual disk volumes on ESXi servers using a version of Darkside ransomware. Additionally, FIN7 has deployed ransomware as the end payload during big game hunting.

T1486.subject: G0059
T1486.text: Magic Hound has used BitLocker and DiskCryptor to encrypt targeted workstations.

T1486.subject: G0061
T1486.text: FIN8 has deployed ransomware such as Ragnar Locker, White Rabbit, and attempted to execute Noberus on compromised networks.

T1486.subject: G0082
T1486.text: APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256.

T1486.subject: G0092
T1486.text: TA505 has used a wide variety of ransomware, such as Clop, Locky, Jaff, Bart, Philadelphia, and GlobeImposter, to encrypt victim files and demand a ransom payment.

T1486.subject: G0096
T1486.text: APT41 used a ransomware called Encryptor RaaS to encrypt files on the targeted systems and provide a ransom note to the user. APT41 also used Microsoft Bitlocker to encrypt workstations and Jetico’s BestCrypt to encrypt servers.

T1486.subject: G0119
T1486.text: Indrik Spider has encrypted domain-controlled systems using BitPaymer. Additionally, Indrik Spider used PsExec to execute a ransomware script.

T1486.subject: G1015
T1486.text: Scattered Spider has used BlackCat and DragonForce ransomware to encrypt files including on VMWare ESXi servers.

T1486.subject: G1024
T1486.text: Akira encrypts files in victim environments as part of ransomware operations.

T1486.subject: G1032
T1486.text: INC Ransom has used INC Ransomware to encrypt victim's data.

T1486.subject: G1036
T1486.text: Moonstone Sleet has deployed ransomware in victim environments.

T1486.subject: G1043
T1486.text: BlackByte has encrypted victim files for ransom. Early versions of BlackByte ransomware used a common key for encryption, but later versions use unique keys per victim.

T1486.subject: G1046
T1486.text: Storm-1811 is a financially-motivated entity linked to the deployment of Black Basta ransomware in victim environments.

T1486.subject: G1050
T1486.text: Water Galura has encrypted files on victim networks through the generation of Qilin ransomware payloads.

T1486.subject: G1051
T1486.text: Medusa Group has encrypted files using AES-256 encryption which then appends the file extension “.medusa” to encrypted files and leaves a ransomware note named “!READ_ME_MEDUSA!!!.txt.”

T1486.subject: G1053
T1486.text: Storm-0501 has encrypted files in victim environments using ransomware as a service (RaaS) including Sabbath, Hive, BlackCat, Hunters International, LockBit 3.0 and Embargo ransomware.

T1486.subject: G1055
T1486.text: VOID MANTICORE has utilized legitimate disk encryption utilities to increase likelihood of encrypting system drives and reduce system recovery efforts.

T1486.subject: G1056
T1486.text: TeamPCP has deployed ransomware and has announced partnerships with ransomware groups including Vect and CipherForce in online criminal forums.

T1486.subject: S0140
T1486.text: Shamoon has an operational mode for encrypting data instead of overwriting it.

T1486.subject: S0242
T1486.text: SynAck encrypts the victims machine followed by asking the victim to pay a ransom.

T1486.subject: S0341
T1486.text: Xbash has maliciously encrypted victim's database systems and demanded a cryptocurrency ransom be paid.

T1486.subject: S0366
T1486.text: WannaCry encrypts user files and demands that a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files.

T1486.subject: S0368
T1486.text: NotPetya encrypts user files and disk structures like the MBR with 2048-bit RSA.

T1486.subject: S0370
T1486.text: SamSam encrypts victim files using RSA-2048 encryption and demands a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files.

T1486.subject: S0372
T1486.text: LockerGoga has encrypted files, including core Windows OS files, using RSA-OAEP MGF1 and then demanded Bitcoin be paid for the decryption key.

T1486.subject: S0389
T1486.text: JCry has encrypted files and demanded Bitcoin to decrypt those files.

T1486.subject: S0400
T1486.text: RobbinHood will search for an RSA encryption key and then perform its encryption process on the system files.

T1486.subject: S0446
T1486.text: Ryuk has used a combination of symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption to encrypt files. Files have been encrypted with their own AES key and given a file extension of .RYK. Encrypted directories have had a ransom note of RyukReadMe.txt written to the directory.

T1486.subject: S0449
T1486.text: Maze has disrupted systems by encrypting files on targeted machines, claiming to decrypt files if a ransom payment is made. Maze has used the ChaCha algorithm, based on Salsa20, and an RSA algorithm to encrypt files.

T1486.subject: S0457
T1486.text: Netwalker can encrypt files on infected machines to extort victims.

T1486.subject: S0481
T1486.text: Ragnar Locker encrypts files on the local machine and mapped drives prior to displaying a note demanding a ransom.

T1486.subject: S0496
T1486.text: REvil can encrypt files on victim systems and demands a ransom to decrypt the files.

T1486.subject: S0554
T1486.text: Egregor can encrypt all non-system files using a hybrid AES-RSA algorithm prior to displaying a ransom note.

T1486.subject: S0556
T1486.text: Pay2Key can encrypt data on victim's machines using RSA and AES algorithms in order to extort a ransom payment for decryption.

T1486.subject: S0570
T1486.text: BitPaymer can import a hard-coded RSA 1024-bit public key, generate a 128-bit RC4 key for each file, and encrypt the file in place, appending .locked to the filename.

T1486.subject: S0575
T1486.text: Conti can use CreateIoCompletionPort(), PostQueuedCompletionStatus(), and GetQueuedCompletionPort() to rapidly encrypt files, excluding those with the extensions of .exe, .dll, and .lnk. It has used a different AES-256 encryption key per file with a bundled RAS-4096 public encryption key that is unique for each victim. Conti can use “Windows Restart Manager”

T1486.subject: S0576
T1486.text: MegaCortex has used the open-source library, Mbed Crypto, and generated AES keys to carry out the file encryption process.

T1486.subject: S0583
T1486.text: Pysa has used RSA and AES-CBC encryption algorithm to encrypt a list of targeted file extensions.

T1486.subject: S0595
T1486.text: ThiefQuest encrypts a set of file extensions on a host, deletes the original files, and provides a ransom note with no contact information.

T1486.subject: S0605
T1486.text: EKANS uses standard encryption library functions to encrypt files.

T1486.subject: S0606
T1486.text: Bad Rabbit has encrypted files and disks using AES-128-CBC and RSA-2048.

T1486.subject: S0607
T1486.text: KillDisk has a ransomware component that encrypts files with an AES key that is also RSA-1028 encrypted.

T1486.subject: S0611
T1486.text: Clop can encrypt files using AES, RSA, and RC4 and will add the ".clop" extension to encrypted files.

T1486.subject: S0612
T1486.text: WastedLocker can encrypt data and leave a ransom note.

T1486.subject: S0616
T1486.text: DEATHRANSOM can use public and private key pair encryption to encrypt files for ransom payment.

T1486.subject: S0617
T1486.text: HELLOKITTY can use an embedded RSA-2048 public key to encrypt victim data for ransom.

T1486.subject: S0618
T1486.text: FIVEHANDS can use an embedded NTRU public key to encrypt data for ransom.

T1486.subject: S0625
T1486.text: Cuba has the ability to encrypt system data and add the ".cuba" extension to encrypted files.

T1486.subject: S0638
T1486.text: Babuk can use ChaCha8 and ECDH to encrypt data.

T1486.subject: S0639
T1486.text: Seth-Locker can encrypt files on a targeted system, appending them with the suffix .seth.

T1486.subject: S0640
T1486.text: Avaddon encrypts the victim system using a combination of AES256 and RSA encryption schemes.

T1486.subject: S0654
T1486.text: ProLock can encrypt files on a compromised host with RC6, and encrypts the key with RSA-1024.

T1486.subject: S0658
T1486.text: XCSSET performs AES-CBC encryption on files under ~/Documents, ~/Downloads, and ~/Desktop with a fixed key and renames files to give them a .enc extension. Only files with sizes less than 500MB are encrypted.

T1486.subject: S0659
T1486.text: Diavol has encrypted files using an RSA key though the `CryptEncrypt` API and has appended filenames with ".lock64".

T1486.subject: S1033
T1486.text: DCSrv has encrypted drives using the core encryption mechanism from DiskCryptor.

T1486.subject: S1053
T1486.text: AvosLocker has encrypted files and network resources using AES-256 and added an `.avos`, `.avos2`, or `.AvosLinux` extension to filenames.

T1486.subject: S1058
T1486.text: Prestige has leveraged the CryptoPP C++ library to encrypt files on target systems using AES and appended filenames with `.enc`.

T1486.subject: S1068
T1486.text: BlackCat has the ability to encrypt Windows devices, Linux devices, and VMWare instances.

T1486.subject: S1070
T1486.text: Black Basta can encrypt files with the ChaCha20 cypher and using a multithreaded process to increase speed. Black Basta has also encrypted files while the victim system is in safe mode, appending `.basta` upon completion.

T1486.subject: S1073
T1486.text: Royal uses a multi-threaded encryption process that can partially encrypt targeted files with the OpenSSL library and the AES256 algorithm.

T1486.subject: S1096
T1486.text: Cheerscrypt can encrypt data on victim machines using a Sosemanuk stream cipher with an Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH) generated key.

T1486.subject: S1111
T1486.text: DarkGate can deploy follow-on ransomware payloads.

T1486.subject: S1129
T1486.text: Akira can encrypt victim filesystems for financial extortion purposes including through the use of the ChaCha20 and ChaCha8 stream ciphers.

T1486.subject: S1133
T1486.text: Apostle creates new, encrypted versions of files then deletes the originals, with the new filenames consisting of a random GUID and ".lock" for an extension.

T1486.subject: S1137
T1486.text: Moneybird targets a common set of file types such as documents, certificates, and database files for encryption while avoiding executable, dynamic linked libraries, and similar items.

T1486.subject: S1139
T1486.text: INC Ransomware can encrypt data on victim systems, including through the use of partial encryption and multi-threading to speed encryption.

T1486.subject: S1150
T1486.text: ROADSWEEP can RC4 encrypt content in blocks on targeted systems.

T1486.subject: S1162
T1486.text: Playcrypt encrypts files on targeted hosts with an AES-RSA hybrid encryption, encrypting every other file portion of 0x100000 bytes.

T1486.subject: S1178
T1486.text: ShrinkLocker uses the legitimate BitLocker application to encrypt victim files for ransom.

T1486.subject: S1180
T1486.text: BlackByte Ransomware is ransomware using a shared key across victims for encryption.

T1486.subject: S1181
T1486.text: BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware is a ransomware variant associated with BlackByte operations.

T1486.subject: S1191
T1486.text: Megazord can encrypt files on targeted Windows hosts leaving them with a ".powerranges" file extension.

T1486.subject: S1194
T1486.text: The Akira _v2 encryptor targets the `/vmfs/volumes/` path by default and can use the rust-crypto 0.2.36 library crate for the encryption processes.

T1486.subject: S1199
T1486.text: LockBit 2.0 can use standard AES and elliptic-curve cryptography algorithms to encrypt victim data.

T1486.subject: S1202
T1486.text: LockBit 3.0 can encrypt targeted data using the AES-256, ChaCha20, or RSA-2048 algorithms.

T1486.subject: S1212
T1486.text: RansomHub can use Elliptic Curve Encryption to encrypt files on targeted systems. RansomHub can also skip content at regular intervals (ex. encrypt 1 MB, skip 3 MB) to optomize performance and enable faster encryption for large files.

T1486.subject: S1242
T1486.text: Qilin can use AES-256 or ChaCha20 for domain-wide encryption of victim servers and workstations and RSA-4096 or RSA-2048 to secure generated encryption keys.

T1486.subject: S1244
T1486.text: Medusa Ransomware has encrypted files using AES-256 encryption, which then appends the file extension “.medusa” to encrypted files and leaves a ransomware note named “!READ_ME_MEDUSA!!!.txt.”

T1486.subject: S1247
T1486.text: Embargo has the ability to encrypt files with the ChaCha20 and Curve25519 cryptographic algorithms. Embargo also has the ability to encrypt system data and add a random six-letter extension consisting of hexadecimal characters such as ".b58eeb" or “.3d828a” to encrypted files.

T1486.subject: S9020
T1486.text: LODEINFO can incorporate a ransom command to encrypt specified files and folders.

T1489.text: Lazarus Group has stopped the MSExchangeIS service to render Exchange contents inaccessible to users.

T1489.subject: G0034
T1489.text: Sandworm Team attempts to stop the MSSQL Windows service to ensure successful encryption of locked files.

T1489.subject: G0094
T1489.text: Kimsuky has disabled actively running virtual environments using the `KillMe` function to include VMware, Microsoft Hypervisors, and VirtualBox.

T1489.subject: G0102
T1489.text: Wizard Spider has used taskkill.exe and net.exe to stop backup, catalog, cloud, and other services prior to network encryption.

T1489.subject: G0119
T1489.text: Indrik Spider has used PsExec to stop services prior to the execution of ransomware.

T1489.subject: G1004
T1489.text: LAPSUS$ has shut down virtual machines from within a victim's on-premise VMware ESXi infrastructure.

T1489.subject: G1051
T1489.text: Medusa Group has terminated services related to backups, security, databases, communication, filesharing and websites.

T1489.subject: S0365
T1489.text: Olympic Destroyer uses the API call ChangeServiceConfigW to disable all services on the affected system.

T1489.subject: S0366
T1489.text: WannaCry attempts to kill processes associated with Exchange, Microsoft SQL Server, and MySQL to make it possible to encrypt their data stores.

T1489.subject: S0400
T1489.text: RobbinHood stops 181 Windows services on the system before beginning the encryption process.

T1489.subject: S0431
T1489.text: HotCroissant has the ability to stop services on the infected host.

T1489.subject: S0446
T1489.text: Ryuk has called kill.bat for stopping services, disabling services and killing processes.

T1489.subject: S0449
T1489.text: Maze has stopped SQL services to ensure it can encrypt any database.

T1489.subject: S0457
T1489.text: Netwalker can terminate system processes and services, some of which relate to backup software.

T1489.subject: S0481

T1685.subject: S0689
T1685.text: WhisperGate can download and execute AdvancedRun.exe to disable the Windows Defender Theat Protection service and set an exclusion path for the C:\ drive.

T1685.subject: S0692
T1685.text: SILENTTRINITY's `amsiPatch.py` module can disable Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) functions.

T1685.subject: S0695
T1685.text: Donut can patch Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI), Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP), as well as exit-related Native API functions to avoid process termination.

T1685.subject: S0697
T1685.text: HermeticWiper has the ability to set the `HKLM:\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\CrashControl\CrashDumpEnabled` Registry key to `0` in order to disable crash dumps.

T1685.subject: S1048
T1685.text: macOS.OSAMiner has searched for the Activity Monitor process in the System Events process list and kills the process if running. macOS.OSAMiner also searches the operating system's `install.log` for apps matching its hardcoded list, killing all matching process names.

T1685.subject: S1063
T1685.text: Brute Ratel C4 has the ability to hide memory artifacts and to patch Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) and the Anti Malware Scan Interface (AMSI).

T1685.subject: S1065
T1685.text: Woody RAT has suppressed all error reporting by calling `SetErrorMode` with 0x8007 as a parameter.

T1685.subject: S1097
T1685.text: HUI Loader has the ability to disable Windows Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) and Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) functions.

T1685.subject: S1111
T1685.text: DarkGate will terminate processes associated with several security software products if identified during execution.

T1685.subject: S1114
T1685.text: ZIPLINE can add itself to the exclusion list for the Ivanti Connect Secure Integrity Checker Tool if the `--exclude` parameter is passed by the `tar` process.

T1685.subject: S1130
T1685.text: Raspberry Robin can add an exception to Microsoft Defender that excludes the entire main drive from anti-malware scanning to evade detection.

T1685.subject: S1135
T1685.text: MultiLayer Wiper removes the Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) service from infected devices along with all present shadow copies.

T1685.subject: S1169
T1685.text: Mango contains an unused capability to block endpoint security solutions from loading user-mode code hooks via a DLL in a specified process by using the `UpdateProcThreadAttribute API` to set the `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_MITIGATION_POLICY` to `PROCESS_CREATION_MITIGATION_POLICY_BLOCK_NON_MICROSOFT_BINARIES_ALWAYS_ON` for an identified process.

T1685.subject: S1178
T1685.text: ShrinkLocker disables protectors used to secure the BitLocker encryption key on victim systems.

T1685.subject: S1180
T1685.text: BlackByte Ransomware adds .JS and .EXE extensions to the Microsoft Defender exclusion list. BlackByte Ransomware terminates and removes the Raccine anti-ransomware utility.

T1685.subject: S1184
T1685.text: BOLDMOVE can disable the Fortinet daemons `moglogd` and `syslogd` to evade detection and logging.

T1685.subject: S1199
T1685.text: LockBit 2.0 can disable firewall rules and anti-malware and monitoring software including Windows Defender.

T1685.subject: S1200
T1685.text: StealBit can configure processes to not display certain Windows error messages by through use of the `NtSetInformationProcess`.

T1685.subject: S1202
T1685.text: LockBit 3.0 can disable security tools to evade detection including Windows Defender.

T1685.subject: S1206
T1685.text: JumbledPath can impair logging on all devices used along its connection path to compromised hosts.

T1685.subject: S1207
T1685.text: XLoader loads a copy of NTDLL to evade hooks from security monitoring tools on this library. XLoader can add the path of its executable to the Microsoft Defender exclusion list.

T1685.subject: S1213
T1685.text: Lumma Stealer has attempted to bypass Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by removing the string “AmsiScanBuffer” from the “clr.dll” module in memory to prevent it from being called.

T1685.subject: S1234
T1685.text: SplatCloak has identified and disabled API callback features of Windows Defender and Kaspersky.

T1685.subject: S1240
T1685.text: RedLine Stealer can disable security software and update services.

T1685.subject: S1242
T1685.text: Qilin can terminate antivirus-related processes and services.

T1685.subject: S1244
T1685.text: Medusa Ransomware has terminated antivirus services utilizing the gaze.exe executable. Medusa Ransomware has also terminated antivirus services utilizing PowerShell scripts.

T1685.subject: S9008
T1685.text: Shai-Hulud has replaced DNS configuration from `/tmp/resolved.conf` in order to gain control of network-level control within CI environments and has flushed iptables rules using `sudo iptables -F OUTPUT` and `sudo iptables -F DOCKER-USER`.

T1685.subject: S9013
T1685.text: DRYHOOK has killed all instances of the `cgi-server` process in order for the modified Perl module to be activated.

T1685.subject: S9014
T1685.text: PHASEJAM has modified Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and blocks the system upgrades by altering the DSUpgrade.pm file.

T1685.subject: S9017
T1685.text: DCRAT can patch Microsoft’s Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) to evade detection.

T1685.subject: S9019
T1685.text: PureCrypter has executed `Set-MpPreference -ExclusionPath` to exclude files or folders from Windows Defender scans.

T1685.subject: S9024
T1685.text: SPAWNCHIMERA has modified the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool to evade detection.

T1685.subject: S9039
T1685.text: LazyWiper can disable Microsoft Windows Defender Real-Time Monitoring with the `Set-MpPreference` cmdlet.

T1685.005.subject: C0014
T1685.005.text: During Operation Wocao, the threat actors deleted all Windows system and security event logs using `/Q /c wevtutil cl system` and `/Q /c wevtutil cl security`.

T1685.005.subject: C0060
T1685.005.text: During Operation AkaiRyū, MirrorFace cleared Windows event logs post compromise.

T1685.005.subject: G0007
T1685.005.text: APT28 has cleared event logs, including by using the commands wevtutil cl System and wevtutil cl Security.

T1685.005.subject: G0035
T1685.005.text: Dragonfly has cleared Windows event logs and other logs produced by tools they used, including system, security, terminal services, remote services, and audit logs. The actors also deleted specific Registry keys.

T1685.005.subject: G0050
T1685.005.text: APT32 has cleared select event log entries.

T1685.005.subject: G0053
T1685.005.text: FIN5 has cleared event logs from victims.

T1685.005.subject: G0061
T1685.005.text: FIN8 has cleared logs during post compromise cleanup activities.

T1685.005.subject: G0082
T1685.005.text: APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system.

T1685.005.subject: G0096
T1685.005.text: APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by clearing Windows security and system events.

T1685.005.subject: G0114
T1685.005.text: Chimera has cleared event logs on compromised hosts.

T1685.005.subject: G0119
T1685.005.text: Indrik Spider has used Cobalt Strike to empty log files. Additionally, Indrik Spider has cleared all event logs using `wevutil`.

T1685.005.subject: G0125
T1685.005.text: HAFNIUM has cleared actor-performed actions from logs.

T1685.005.subject: G0143
T1685.005.text: Aquatic Panda clears Windows Event Logs following activity to evade defenses.

T1685.005.subject: G1017
T1685.005.text: Volt Typhoon has selectively cleared Windows Event Logs, system logs, and other technical artifacts to remove evidence of intrusion activity.

T1685.005.subject: G1040
T1685.005.text: Play has used tools to remove log files on targeted systems.

T1685.005.subject: G1054
T1685.005.text: MirrorFace has deleted Windows event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0032
T1685.005.text: gh0st RAT is able to wipe event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0089
T1685.005.text: The BlackEnergy component KillDisk is capable of deleting Windows Event Logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0182
T1685.005.text: FinFisher clears the system event logs using OpenEventLog/ClearEventLog APIs .

T1685.005.subject: S0192
T1685.005.text: Pupy has a module to clear event logs with PowerShell.

T1685.005.subject: S0203
T1685.005.text: Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can clear all system event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0242
T1685.005.text: SynAck clears event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0253
T1685.005.text: RunningRAT contains code to clear event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0365
T1685.005.text: Olympic Destroyer will attempt to clear the System and Security event logs using wevtutil.

T1685.005.subject: S0368
T1685.005.text: NotPetya uses wevtutil to clear the Windows event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0412
T1685.005.text: ZxShell has a command to clear system event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0532
T1685.005.text: Lucifer can clear and remove event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0607
T1685.005.text: KillDisk deletes Application, Security, Setup, and System Windows Event Logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0645
T1685.005.text: Wevtutil can be used to clear system and security event logs from the system.

T1685.005.subject: S0688
T1685.005.text: Meteor can use Wevtutil to remove Security, System and Application Event Viewer logs.

T1685.005.subject: S0697
T1685.005.text: HermeticWiper can overwrite the `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs` file on a targeted system.

T1685.005.subject: S0698
T1685.005.text: HermeticWizard has the ability to use `wevtutil cl system` to clear event logs.

T1685.005.subject: S1060
T1685.005.text: Mafalda can delete Windows Event logs by invoking the `OpenEventLogW` and `ClearEventLogW` functions.

T1685.005.subject: S1068
T1685.005.text: BlackCat can clear Windows event logs using `wevtutil.exe`.

T1685.005.subject: S1133
T1685.005.text: Apostle will attempt to delete all event logs on a victim machine following file wipe activity.

T1685.005.subject: S1135
T1685.005.text: MultiLayer Wiper removes Windows event logs during execution.

T1685.005.subject: S1159
T1685.005.text: DUSTTRAP can delete infected system log information.

T1685.005.subject: S1178
T1685.005.text: ShrinkLocker calls Wevtutil to clear the Windows PowerShell and Microsoft-Windows-Powershell/Operational logs.

T1685.005.subject: S1199
T1685.005.text: LockBit 2.0 can delete log files through the use of wevtutil.

T1685.005.subject: S1202
T1685.005.text: LockBit 3.0 can delete log files on targeted systems.

T1685.005.subject: S1212
T1685.005.text: RansomHub can delete events from the Security, System, and Application logs.

T1685.005.subject: S1242
T1685.005.text: Qilin has the ability to clear Windows Event Logs.
